newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Millions vote in Moroccan first-step reform election.
newsitem.headline: Millions vote in Moroccan first-step reform election.

text.p: Moroccans voted on Friday in local elections intended to give more powers to rural regions to improve living standards and lay the basis for wider democracy in the North African country.

"The local councils from now on will form the base of the national pyramid of democracy," said the independent le Quotidien magazine, referring to planned reforms under a constitution approved in September 1996.

All polling stations closed by 8 p.m. (2000 GMT) after many stayed open for an extra two hours to maximise voting and state television said counting had started. Final results were expected by early Saturday.
The Interior Ministry said 59 percent of the electorate of more that 13 million had voted by 5 p.m.

Opposition parties campaigned all out to try to change three decades of rule at all levels by pro-government parties after King Hassan said on television last year that he was fed up with vote-rigging charges and personally pledged honest elections.
In a sign of the authorities' pledged "transparency", clear plastic ballot boxes were used for the first time.

The elections were contested by a dozen parties, most of which linked up in three main alliances -- the opposition Koutla, the pro-government rightist Wifaq group and a centre-right group led by the Independent National Rally.

Under the new constitution, the 1,547 local councils emerging from Friday's vote will later this year select three-fifths of the members of a new upper house of parliament. Morocco will then have two assemblies instead of the current single 333-seat body.

"The importance of Friday's polls lies in the fact that future communal representatives will hold three-fifths of the upper house," said Mohamed El Yazghi, a leading figure of the opposition Socialist Union of People's Forces (USFP).
Under planned decentralisation, regional councils will also have more money and power to push development projects to end a disparity between town and country.
About half of the population of 28 million live in the countryside and have higher illiteracy rates, poorer health and lower living standards than people in the cities.
More than 100,000 candidates stood for around 25,000 seats on the councils. Pro-government and centre-right parties won about two-thirds of the seats in a 1992 ballot.

At Lycee Moulay Youssef voting station near the Royal Palace in Rabat, Fatima Hamdi, a teacher in her early 20s, said: "I decided to vote for the USFP because I want a real political change...My generation is fed up with right-wing parties running the councils since independence in 1956."
